conversation.content:
Good morning — I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya Bennett, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mothers. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, especially over the past seven days.

There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your immediate safety. We’ll go through ten gentle questions; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll take it at your pace. When you’re ready, we can begin.

To start:  
**Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things — or has that felt difficult?**
I’ve had moments where I’ll smile if someone makes a joke, but it feels forced—like I’m going through the motions. Most of the time I’m just too tired or low to find anything genuinely funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I wish I could say that. A few times my partner tried to joke to lighten the mood, and I gave a little laugh, but it felt kind of hollow—like I was pretending more than actually feeling it. Most days nothing feels funny; I’m either too worried or just... flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like another chore. I’ll think “I should want to do that,” but the spark just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—like I’m missing some “mom instinct” everyone else has. Yesterday she wouldn’t nap, and I sat there crying, telling myself it’s my fault for not reading her cues properly. I know, rationally, babies just cry, but I still feel like I’m failing her somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not gaining enough weight, even though the pediatrician said she’s fine. Or I’ll lie down and picture her stopping breathing in the bassinet, so I have to check her every few minutes. There’s no real reason—it’s like my mind keeps jumping to the worst thing that could happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… it hits out of nowhere. A couple nights ago I was rocking the baby in the dark and suddenly felt like I couldn’t breathe—my chest got tight, heart pounding, like something awful was about to happen even though we were just sitting there. It passed after a minute, but it left me shaky. It’s happened a few times this week, always when everything’s actually quiet.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, the next is due, or there’s laundry piled up, or I need to pump, and I can’t keep up. I’ll look around the apartment and just feel this weight on my chest—like I’m drowning in stuff that needs doing and I’ll never catch up. Sometimes I sit on the floor while she naps and stare at the mess, too overwhelmed to even start.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. Even when the baby’s finally down, my mind keeps spinning—did I sterilize the bottles right, is she breathing, am I doing any of this right—and I can’t settle. I’ll lie there for an hour or more, then jerk awake at every little sound. Some nights I only get three broken hours, and I dread the next feed because I’m already exhausted.
I have felt sad or miserable

That’s pretty much my baseline lately. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a cloud parked over me. I’ll look at my daughter and feel love, but it’s muffled by this constant sadness I can’t shake. Little things make me tear up—seeing another mom looking put-together at the store, or a diaper commercial, anything really. It’s like the happy version of me is stuck behind a thick wall of “blah” and I don’t know how to get her back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened three times this week. Yesterday I just sat in the rocker with her asleep on my chest and the tears started rolling—no real trigger, just this wave of sadness. I try to keep quiet so she won’t wake up, but sometimes I can’t hold it in. It feels like the only release I get, even though I hate that I’m crying over nothing I can name.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I feel low, but I could never leave my baby like that. I just want the sadness and the worry to lift, not to disappear.

You've painted a very clear picture of how heavy life has felt since your baby arrived. Despite the love you feel for your daughter, each day seems covered by a thick, joyless fog: laughter feels forced, simple pleasures have vanished, and even quiet moments trigger waves of worry or sudden panic. You blame yourself when your baby fusses, cry without warning, and sit frozen amid chores that feel impossible to start. Sleep brings little rest because your mind races with fears that something terrible might happen. You are exhausted, overwhelmed, and painfully aware that the happy version of yourself seems unreachable right now.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes inability to genuinely laugh, feeling flat and worried, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('I do that a lot') with specific examples of feeling responsible for baby's fussiness and napping issues, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient experiences near-daily, intrusive worries without real cause, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic symptoms (chest tightness, pounding heart, dread) occurring repeatedly without triggers, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to keep up, and physical sensation of drowning, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption driven by anxious rumination and dread, consistent with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Response describes pervasive, daily sadness that overshadows joy and triggers frequent tears, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes this week with no identifiable trigger, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 places you well above the threshold indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Your descriptions map onto core criteria: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness, recurrent anxiety and panic, fatigue, and sleep disturbance. High scores on guilt, overwhelm, and impaired functioning signal significant impairment. Because item 10 was scored 0, immediate self-harm risk is not indicated, but severity still warrants urgent evaluation and support. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>OB-GYN</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>interpersonal therapy</med>, or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Involve a trusted adult to help with night feeds so you can obtain four to five hours of uninterrupted sleep
4. Reach out today to local or online <med>postpartum support groups</med> (e.g., Postpartum Support International warmline 1-800-944-4PPD)
5. Schedule daily 15-minute mood check-ins with your partner or friend; agree on a signal if feelings worsen
6. Use brief grounding techniques (slow breathing, naming five objects you see) when <sym>panic sensations</sym> appear
7. Create a simple care plan: one shower, one balanced meal, one five-minute outdoor breath of fresh air daily
8. Arrange follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 10-item Edinburgh Plus Anxiety Cues

Presenting symptoms  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Marked guilt/self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Daily free-floating anxiety, catastrophic worries, nocturnal checking (Q4)  
- Acute panic-type episodes (tight chest, breathlessness) without clear trigger (Q5)  
- Overwhelm, feeling “drowning” in tasks, difficulty initiating care activities (Q6)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance problems linked to intrusive worries (Q7)  
- Diminished positive affect even when desired (e.g., laughing with partner) (Q1)

Pattern  
Symptoms present most days × ≥2 weeks, cause subjective distress and functional interference with infant care and self-care. No current suicidal or self-harm ideation; protective factor = strong infant attachment (Q10).

Screening significance  
High endorsement consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious features (postpartum onset) and co-occurring panic spectrum symptoms; meets threshold for further diagnostic evaluation and safety plan.

Risk factors noted  
Primiparity, intense maternal self-expectations, sleep deprivation, absence of perceived social comparison (“put-together” moms).

Recommendation  
Urgent referral for comprehensive perinatal mental health assessment; consider same-week appointment.
